details: The three principles of radiation protection: (1) TIME: reduce exposure duration; dose = dose rate × time; halving time → halving dose; example: at 100 µSv/hr: 1hr → 100 µSv; 30min → 50 µSv; 6min → 10 µSv; CEZ application: roof worker 90s limit at 1000+ R/hr → ~25 mSv/shift; if 5min → 140 mSv; (2) DISTANCE: dose rate follows inverse square law (point source): H = H₀ × (d₀/d)²; doubling distance → quarter dose; at 1m from source: 1000 µSv/hr; at 2m: 250 µSv/hr; at 4m: 62.5 µSv/hr; CEZ application: Elephant's Foot 1986 at 1m: 10,000 R/hr; at 3m: 1100 R/hr; at 10m: 100 R/hr → time to lethal dose changes from 30s to 5min to 50min; (3) SHIELDING: interpose attenuating material between source and person; HVL (half-value layer): material thickness for 50% attenuation; lead HVL for Cs-137 662 keV gamma: 7mm; concrete HVL: 5.5cm; water HVL: 9.8cm; example: 10 HVL lead = 70mm = 1024× reduction (factor 2¹⁰)
chernobyl_application: ALARA principle: As Low As Reasonably Achievable; regulatory philosophy: dose reduction to level below limits AND reduced further if practical; two components: (1) Dose below regulatory limit (20 mSv/yr occupational; 1 mSv/yr public); (2) THEN further optimization: is the dose justified? Can it be reasonably reduced? Tools: dose monitoring; work planning (mock-up training); remote handling; shielding installation; ventilation; contamination control; Chernobyl ALARA application: NSC decommissioning workers: dose planning uses 3D MCNP models to identify: highest-dose work steps; optimal work sequence; required shielding; remote tools vs hands-on; target: <5 mSv/yr average for decommissioning workers (EBRD requirement = below 20 mSv/yr statutory limit; further optimization to ALARA)

details: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) for radiological work: CONTAMINATION CONTROL (vs dose reduction): purpose: prevent skin/internal contamination; NOT for external gamma shielding (clothing provides no significant gamma protection); PPE for contamination: (1) Coveralls (tyvek or cotton): prevents skin deposition; laundered/disposed between shifts; (2) Gloves (double latex): protects hands; highest contamination pathway; (3) Shoe covers/booties: prevents spread of contamination; (4) Face shield/goggles: protects eyes from aerosol; (5) Respiratory protection: half-face respirator (PF=10): 10× reduction of inhalation; full-face respirator (PF=50-100); SCBA (self-contained breathing apparatus; PF=10,000): used in high-activity aerosol environments; P100 filter: 99.97% efficiency for particles >0.3µm; Chernobyl liquidators 1986: mostly received: cloth respirator (PF<2; essentially useless); some: military gas masks (PF=1000+); most workers: inadequate respiratory protection especially for fine aerosol (AMAD 0.3µm from volatile Cs-137)
chernobyl_application: Respiratory protection for Cs-137 aerosol: Cs-137 aerosol AMAD 0.3-1 µm: P100 filter needed (97% efficiency); ineffective protection: surgical mask (PF~2); cotton cloth (~1.5); dust mask (PF~5); EFFECTIVE: N95/P100 half-face (PF 10-50); full-face P100 (PF 50-100); 1986 most liquidators used cotton masks = inadequate; however: inhalation dose at Chernobyl << external gamma dose for most workers (exceptions: firefighters at fire scene = inhalation important); dose contribution breakdown: 1986 firefighters (at fire plume): inhalation 30-40%; external gamma 60-70%; 1986 liquidators (away from fire): inhalation <5%; external gamma >95%; therefore: PPE (no gamma shielding) had limited practical dose reduction despite important contamination prevention role

details: Radiation area classification for workplaces: IAEA GSG-7 (2018): Occupational Radiation Protection; area classification: (1) Controlled area: dose rate could exceed 6 µSv/hr (3 mSv/yr if continuously occupied); requires: entry control; dosimetry; contamination monitoring; access log; (2) Supervised area: dose rate 1-6 µSv/hr; periodic monitoring; (3) Uncontrolled: <1 µSv/hr; standard public area; CEZ area classification: Exclusion Zone entire area: Controlled (restricted entry; permits required); NPP site: Controlled with sub-zones; Yellow Zone (lowest restriction): 0.2-0.5 µSv/hr; Orange Zone: 0.5-2 µSv/hr; Red Zone: >2 µSv/hr; Black Zone (restricted access, written permit + dosimetry): >10 µSv/hr; NSC interior: Controlled/Restricted; Elephant's Foot area: Black Zone (inaccessible; >1000 µSv/hr in 2026); comparison to routine hospitals: CT scanner operator area: Controlled (2-5 µSv/hr)
chernobyl_application: Area classification in practice: SaveEcoBot sensor data April 2026: Prypiat 4.932 µSv/hr = Red Zone (>2 µSv/hr); Chernobyl city 0.209 µSv/hr = Yellow Zone (0.2-0.5 µSv/hr); NPP site boundary 0.6-2 µSv/hr = Orange Zone; Red Forest 2-100+ µSv/hr = Red Zone (hotspot patches = Black Zone); Exclusion Zone entrance gate 0.1-0.3 µSv/hr = Supervised or Controlled; working in Prypiat: dose rate 4.932 µSv/hr × 8hr shift = 39.5 µSv/shift; 250 shifts/yr = 9.9 mSv/yr = below occupational limit (20 mSv/yr) but above public limit; Prypiat NOT habitable for general public (43 mSv/yr continuous) but DOES meet criteria for occupational work with proper monitoring; decommissioning workers already working in similar dose rate areas

details: Whole Body Counter (WBC) and internal dose monitoring: WBC system: array of NaI(Tl) or HPGe detectors surrounding person in shielded room (steel or concrete walls to reduce background); measurement: full body gamma spectrum; Cs-137 662 keV peak measured; detection limit for Cs-137: ~270 Bq (WBC with NaI; 10 min count); ~100 Bq (HPGe; 30 min count); committed effective dose calculation: measured activity (Bq in body) × dose coefficient (Sv/Bq) = committed dose; for Cs-137: 270 Bq × 1.3×10⁻⁸ Sv/Bq = 3.5 nSv (negligible; well below detection significance at 270 Bq = detection limit); occupationally significant WBC reading: >50,000 Bq → committed dose 0.65 mSv; Ukraine: 200,000+ WBC measurements in liquidators; average body burden declining (see cs137_body_burden_ukraine_REAL.csv); autumn peak from mushroom consumption
chernobyl_application: WBC monitoring program Ukraine 2026: Zhytomyr screening center: IAEA-supported; HPGe WBC system; 109,936 persons screened 2009-2018 (see cs137_body_burden_ukraine_REAL.csv); body burden declined 21.6 → 3.0 Bq/kg over period; autumn (September-November) peak: mushroom season → body burden 3-5× higher than spring; wildboar consumption: single meal can add 10,000-50,000 Bq Cs-137 (EU limit 600 Bq/kg; wild boar mean 46,000 Bq/kg); remediation: Prussian Blue (cesium binder) if body burden high; K-rich diet to compete with Cs-137 uptake; body burden trends: consistent with: general population reducing Cs-137 from declining environmental contamination + behavioral changes (fewer contaminated food items consumed); self-settlers (samosely): body burdens 5-10× higher than evacuated population (due to home-produced food)

details: Potassium iodide (KI) thyroid blocking: mechanism: saturate thyroid NIS symporter with stable I-127 → radioactive I-131 cannot be concentrated; dose: adult 100mg KI (1 tablet); child 8-13yr: 65mg (half tablet); child 3-7yr: 65mg; child 1-3yr: 32mg; infant <1yr: 16mg; timing: maximum effectiveness if taken <1hr before radioiodine exposure; 90% blocking if taken 1hr before; 50% if 4hr before; 0% if 8hr after (thyroid already concentrated I-131); contraindications: thyroid disease; iodine allergy (rare; severe thyroid conditions); hypothyroidism patients on levothyroxine: at higher risk (consult physician); side effects: generally minor (GI upset; rare iodism); KI does NOT protect against external gamma; does NOT protect against Cs-137/Sr-90; specific for I-131 thyroid blocking ONLY; duration: 24hr protection per tablet; re-dosing may be needed if exposure continues; maximum age for benefit: <40yr (thyroid cancer risk mainly in young; older adults: low benefit vs risk)
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl KI failure: Soviet Union DID NOT distribute KI to affected populations in 1986; only Poland distributed to 18 million persons within first days; Poland success: no thyroid cancer excess in Polish children (vs 6000+ cases in Belarus/Ukraine/Russia children); cause: (1) KI not distributed from Soviet stocks (stockpiles existed); (2) No public warning = no public KI uptake; (3) Some individuals self-purchased (pharmacies reported KI shortages in Kyiv April 28-30); lesson: pre-positioned KI + public education = essential; IAEA recommendation: KI pre-positioned for: all persons within 3-5km (PAZ); available for 10-30km (UPZ) on emergency distribution; NOT recommended for >40km (benefit-risk unfavorable); post-Chernobyl changes: EU directive: KI stockpiles mandatory for 100km radius in all EU member states; US NRC: 50 mile EPZ KI available; UK: pre-distributed to 2km

details: Radiological decontamination procedures: external skin decontamination: (1) Remove clothing (removes 60-80% of contamination); (2) Shower with soap + water (mild; avoid abrasion = skin barrier damage allows absorption); removes 95%+ of deposited loose contamination; (3) Hair wash (shampoo); (4) Wound decontamination: irrigation with normal saline; avoid introducing contamination deeper; (5) Fixed contamination: in skin pores; some absorption; cannot be removed by washing; internal decontamination: gut: if recent ingestion: emetics or gastric lavage (within 1-2hr); cathartics; Prussian Blue (Cs-137 gut cycling interruption); Ca-DTPA + Zn-DTPA: chelation for Pu/Am/Ce/La (licensed by FDA); timing critical: chelation most effective within hours of internal contamination; lungs: DTPA by inhalation; long-term: lavage if massive inhalation; CEZ vehicle decontamination 1986: trucks; tanks; helicopters; APCs; high-pressure water + chemical decontamination; vehicles still radioactive after 5+ washing cycles (radiation fixed in metals) → vehicle graveyard at Buryakivka (800+ vehicles)
chernobyl_application: Building decontamination: Pripyat buildings 1986-1990: high-pressure water; polymer film (polymerizing foam applied; removed when dry taking dust + particles); acid washing for floors; roof surface replacement; window cleaning; effectiveness: 70-90% dose rate reduction in interior spaces; however: 40yr later natural accumulation of contaminated dust + re-deposition of resuspended particles from outdoors; Chernobyl city: road decontamination: scraping; fresh asphalt; effective (Chernobyl city now <0.3 µSv/hr in streets); Pripyat: partially decontaminated 1986-1990; then: nature reclaimed; building interiors now have secondary contamination from: weathering; window breakage; bird droppings; water ingress; Pripyat 2026 = mix of original 1986 contamination + secondary contamination; overall dose rate 4.932 µSv/hr dominated by soil Cs-137 in immediate surroundings

details: Personal dosimetry technologies: (1) TLD (Thermoluminescent Dosimeter): LiF:Mg,Ti or LiF:Mg,Cu,P crystal; read monthly; ±15% accuracy; current standard in Ukraine/Belarus; (2) OSL (Optically Stimulated Luminescence): aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃:C); read by laser; ±10% accuracy; InLight system (Landauer); can be read and re-read non-destructively; (3) EPD (Electronic Personal Dosimeter): real-time display; alarm at user-set dose rate; can be read during shift; DISADVANTAGE: cannot serve as legal record in most jurisdictions; (4) Film badge: original method; being phased out; sensitive to heat and humidity; (5) RPL (Radiophotoluminescence): silver-activated glass; Japanese method; read by UV fluorescence; ±5% accuracy; OSL advantage: can be re-read (archived record); TLD advantage: cheap; robust; widely deployed; EPD advantage: real-time (worker aware of current dose); liquid scintillation counter: measures H-3 in urine (bioassay for tritium intake)
chernobyl_application: Dosimetry program requirements (IAEA GSG-7): individual dosimetry required for: (1) Controlled area workers; (2) Dose exceeding 1 mSv/yr possible; records: maintained for LIFE of worker + 30 years; data registration: national dose registry; Ukraine: RNMDR (liquidator registry) + SSE CHNPP workers registry; Belarus: similar; dose records: required for: compensation eligibility + medical monitoring; Chernobyl dosimetry failures: KID-2 (1986 pocket ionization chamber; 0-5 rem range; systematically falsified); LESSON: EPD + OSL dual-badge system avoids single-point falsification (harder to falsify both); post-2000 Ukrainian nuclear plant dosimetry: OSL primary + EPD real-time; electronic records; SNRIU audit; dosimetry integrity improved substantially; remaining challenge: CEZ environmental workers on short-term contracts may not receive equivalent monitoring

details: Emergency protective action framework: IAEA GSR Part 7 (2015): emergency planning zones; PAZ (Precautionary Action Zone): 3-5 km from nuclear plant; immediate evacuation upon declared General Emergency; no radiation measurement needed (acting on plant status); UPZ (Urgent Protective Action Zone): 10-30 km; shelter-in-place + KI + evacuation based on actual radiation measurements; EPZ (Emergency Planning Zone): up to 30km for most events; decision criteria: dose projected in PAZ: >10 mSv thyroid or >10 mSv effective → evacuate; shelter reduces dose by 40-90% (house construction dependent); KI blocks thyroid I-131 intake; evacuation: removes entirely from contaminated air; comparison: Soviet 1986 response: Prypiat (3km from NPP) = NOT evacuated until April 27 (36hr after accident); equivalent to PAZ in modern framework = should have been evacuated within 1-2hr; delay = additional dose to 49,360 residents (average 15-20 mSv thyroid dose each from I-131 inhalation; preventable)
chernobyl_application: Modern emergency response: if equivalent accident 2026: EURDEP detects within 30-60 min; notification to IAEA within 1-2hr; PAZ evacuation ordered within 2hr; UPZ shelter + KI distribution within 4hr; based on: meteorological forecast + plume dispersion model (HYSPLIT) + dose rate measurements; Prypiat 2026 (occupied by ~1000 workers): would evacuate to Slavutych (53km SE); evacuation routes maintained; dose in transit: depends on plume direction; Slavutych: out of 30km UPZ; established as safe refuge location since 1991; pre-positioned KI: Ukrainian nuclear plants have KI stored in local pharmacies for 50km radius (post-Chernobyl legal requirement); public: annual notification of nearest distribution point; drill: every 2-3 years; readiness: substantially better than 1986 but war-2022+ has disrupted some exercises
